metadata.title: Estimation and Inference of Heterogeneous Treatment Effects using Random Forests
metadata.abstract: We propose causal forests for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects, and establish asymptotic normality enabling valid confidence intervals.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Classical methods for treatment effect estimation report a single average effect, hiding the fact that a drug or policy may help one subgroup and harm another.
We adapt random forests to estimate how treatment effects vary with covariates, while retaining statistical guarantees.

sections.title: Causal Forests
paragraphs: Each causal tree splits the covariate space to maximize heterogeneity in estimated treatment effects rather than predictive accuracy.
Honesty is the key device: each tree uses one subsample to place splits and a disjoint subsample to estimate effects within leaves, which removes overfitting bias from the estimates.
The forest averages many honest trees grown on random subsamples, and the resulting estimator is pointwise consistent for the true conditional treatment effect.

sections.title: Asymptotic Theory
paragraphs: Under regularity conditions on subsample size and split behavior, the causal forest estimator is asymptotically Gaussian, and its variance can be estimated with the infinitesimal jackknife.
This yields confidence intervals for individual-level treatment effects, which prior forest-based methods could not provide.

sections.title: Experiments
paragraphs: In simulations with strong effect heterogeneity, causal forests outperform nearest-neighbor matching and series estimation in mean squared error.
Coverage of the constructed confidence intervals approaches the nominal level as sample size grows.

figures.caption: Coverage of confidence intervals versus sample size across simulation designs.

citations.title: Random Forests
citations.abstract: Random forests are a combination of tree predictors such that each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently.

citations.title: Recursive Partitioning for Heterogeneous Causal Effects
citations.abstract: We propose honest estimation of treatment effects: one sample selects the partition, an independent sample estimates effects within it.

sections.title: One average hides many truths
sections.hook: What if a drug helps half the patients and harms the other half?
sections.claim: Average treatment effects can be misleading; this paper builds a machine that estimates the effect for each kind of patient.
sections.mechanism: Think of dividing patients into ever finer groups — by age, weight, history — and measuring the treated-versus-control difference inside each group. Causal forests automate that division with trees that split where the effect changes most.

new_terms.definition: A treatment effect that differs across subgroups defined by covariates.

sections.title: Honesty buys validity
sections.hook: Why not just fit a normal random forest to the outcomes?
sections.claim: Splitting and estimating on the same data overfits; using disjoint subsamples for each — honesty — removes that bias.
sections.mechanism: It is the difference between a student writing the exam questions and also grading their own answers, versus two independent students. One subsample chooses where to split; a fresh one measures effects inside each leaf.

new_terms.definition: Using one subsample to choose the model structure and a disjoint one to estimate values within it.

sections.title: Error bars for individuals
sections.hook: Can you trust a per-person effect estimate?
sections.claim: Yes, asymptotically: the estimator is Gaussian around the truth, so confidence intervals are valid.
sections.mechanism: Averaging many honest trees over random subsamples behaves like a well-understood statistical average, and the infinitesimal jackknife estimates its spread — coverage that Figure F1 confirms empirically.
sections.evidence: Supported by S3, S4 and Figure F1.

new_terms.definition: A variance estimator based on how each observation perturbs the ensemble.

key_findings.statement: Forests can estimate individual-level causal effects, not just averages.
key_findings.evidence: Pointwise consistency for the conditional treatment effect.

key_findings.statement: Honesty is what makes the inference valid.
key_findings.evidence: Disjoint split/estimate subsamples remove overfitting bias.
Simulation coverage approaches the nominal level with sample size.

figures.insight: The figure shows the intervals actually cover the truth at close to the promised rate.
